speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Justice whether he is in a position to report to the house on the meeting which has just been held in Washington on the Columbia river project, and more particularly whether he would comment on a statement reported to have been made by a spokesman there that this project is on the borderline now, neither completely approved nor completely rejected.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to deal with the last part of the question first, I have not seen the statement and I do not know who the spokesman purports to be. There have been a number of project sequences under discussion, and I would therefore not care to comment because, as I understand it, the statement of the alleged spokesman refers to "a project". I can only repeat that more than one project sequence has been under consideration.
The meeting took place on Monday and Tuesday of this week and the discussions, as was outlined in a press release, were helpful in further narrowing the areas of difference between the two negotiating teams. A further meeting has been arranged for June 20 and 21 to be held in Ottawa following a further meeting of the international work group which will be working on the data relevant to the various project sequences that have been under discussion.
It is hoped that after that meeting a progress statement at least might be issued. We hope to be in that position although I would not want to be taken as guaranteeing that this will happen.

speechtext: There is some uncertainty as to when congress will rise; but on the basis that it will rise in early July, there is room to hope that in so far as the negotiators are concerned they will be able to report firm recommendations to their governments before that event takes place, and it might even be possible for a tentative agreement or a joint statement of progress to be made by the two governments.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Not an agreement?
[Mr. MacLean (Queens).)

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: Well, I would think that would be running it fairly close, to say we would have a firm agreement before congress rises.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN-U.S. DISCUSSIONS

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to extend its application to the years 1961, 1962 and 1963; and to provide also for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with your permission I should like to make a brief statement on the resolution.
The main purpose of the legislation to be introduced is the extension of assistance to the gold mining industry for an additional three years beyond the present date of expiry of December 31, 1960, without change in the present rate of assistance. A second purpose is to clarify a section of the act for administrative purposes.
You will recall that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was originally passed in 1948 to provide assistance to an industry which was confronted with unusual economic difficulties as a result of the combination of rising costs of production and a fixed market price for its product.
In 1958, at the time the act was extended by this house to apply to the years 1959 and 1960, it was recognized that costs of production had risen to the point where an upward revision of the rates of assistance was necessary to enable the gold mines to maintain operations. The amount of assistance payable for each of the years 1958, 1959 and 1960 was increased by 25 per cent over that calculated under the formula as written into the act.
4224	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
In introducing the 1958 amendment to the act I presented a brief review of the history of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and referred to the continuing economic problems facing the gold mining industry. A review of the present economic position of the gold mines has indicated that of the 40 lode gold mines receiving assistance payments in 1959, 25 mines would be compelled to reduce their scale of operations and perhaps cease operations if aid granted under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act were discontinued.
One of the factors of which the government is mindful in proposing an extension of the operation of the act is the degree of dependence of the gold mining communities upon the gold mining industry. It is evident that termination of assistance payments would lead to difficulties which would have adverse effects on the employment situation in the areas concerned. Notwithstanding the efforts of the mines to reduce costs of production through the use of efficient methods and equipment, it is clear that the need for assistance is no less than it has been in recent years.
The gold mining industry is an important segment of the economic life of our country. It employs over 16,000 men directly, and the population of dependent communities exceeds 70,000 persons. In 1958 the industry expended $106 million in salaries and wages, fuel, electric power, and supplies and equipment. In the same year the industry produced a total of $155 million in gold, most of which was sold to the United States.
It is anticipated that the amount of assistance which will be paid under the provisions of the act with respect to the year 1959 will total $11.7 million. Of this amount, $2,340,000 is attributable to the increase of 25 per cent in the amount of assistance payable. At March 31, 1960 the amount of assistance which had been paid with respect to the year 1958 was, in round figures, $11,138,000, and with respect to the year 1957, $9,680,000. The total amount paid under the act during its 12 years of operation is $131,063,221.51.
Assistance payments are made on gold produced from placer operations as well as on production from lode gold mines. Placer gold is generally recovered from gravel in the beds of streams, whereas lode gold' mines usually mine vein-type gold deposits. Approximately 2,416,000 ounces of fine gold were produced in 1959 from gold mines eligible for assistance payments. Some 65,000 ounces were recovered by placer operations and the balance was produced by lode gold mines.
Of the 4,444,845 ounces of fine gold produced in Canada in 1959, 55 per cent was


produced from gold mines eligible for assistance, 33 per cent from gold mines not eligible for assistance, and 12 per cent was produced as a by-product from base metal mines and was not eligible for assistance.
The amount of assistance a mine receives depends upon both its cost of production and the number of ounces of gold it produces. The formula by which the amount of assistance payable is determined is the product of two thirds of the excess of the average cost per ounce above $26.50, and two thirds of the number of ounces produced by the operator and sold to the mint in that year. This product, increased by 25 per cent, is the assistance payable. A mine receives no assistance if its average cost of production for the year is $26.50 or less.
Fifty three lode gold mines were in operation in 1959. Forty of these mines received cost aid. The remaining 13 were ineligible because of low costs of production. One new mine commenced operation and one mine ceased production during the year.
The purpose of the amendment of subsection 1 of section 3 of the act is to ensure the maintenance of the policy of the government to pay assistance on gold bullion only when it is sold to the Royal Canadian Mint and not on gold bullion that is exported and sold elsewhere. Assistance will continue to be paid on gold exported as contained in ore or concentrates which cannot be economically treated in Canada.
In the maintenance of mining operations over extended periods of time, underground exploration for new ore and the development of known ore must be planned and executed well in advance of the extraction of the ore. In the case of marginal mines, it is especially important that the probable future utility and value of current exploration and development work be carefully assessed. This factor has been taken into consideration in proposing an extension of the operation of the act for a three-year period rather than a two-year period.
It is my hope that this measure will contribute to maintaining the level of gold production in Canada and in this way promote the well-being of our northern gold mining communities.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Last January, when it was announced in the throne speech that the government had decided to extend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for another period of three years after December 1960, the industry in general expressed satisfaction. The news was also well received by communities in Canada whose prosperity and existence depend on gold mining.

In my own constituency, however, where there are nine operating gold mines with some 4,000 gold miners on the payroll, some of the local newspapers expressed the view that the assistance was somewhat short of what it should be on account of the Canadian dollar being at such a high premium.
(Translation):
In its issue of February 18, 1 'Echo de Val d'Or, a local daily, reported a question which had been asked by Dr. H. B. Keevil, chairman of the board of directors of Lamaque Gold Mines Limited, at the annual meeting of that company. Here is the question:
Why could not the Canadian government agree temporarily to buy gold at $35 an ounce in Canadian funds, or alternatively, why could it not base its grants under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act not only on production costs, but also on the lower prices for gold due to fluctuations in the Canadian dollar?
(Text) :
The Rouyn-Noranda Press and Val d'Or Star in their issues of the same date, February 18, 1960 expressed about the same views, and so did some of the other local newspapers.
Mr. Chairman, since its inception in 1948 the act has been amended and extended a number of times. Its main purpose is to assist the Canadian gold mines and the communities depending on that industry. In other words, the act was passed in order to prevent the collapse of the industry and the communities which it supports. Now in its thirteenth year of operation, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been an invaluable interim measure without which very few gold producers or the communities which they support could have remained in operation. Canada has been producing gold for more than 60 years, but the production of the Canadian lode gold mines during 1959 was only about three times that of the year 1900, which is an extraordinary thing.
The historic contribution which the gold mining industry has made to the national economy in earlier and more favourable circumstances in creating new wealth, affording steady employment, stimulating other industries and opening up and developing northern Canada by establishing important towns and communities is a well-known matter of record. Equally well known to the Canadian people are the adverse economic factors with which the industry has had to battle since during the last world war. These have been discussed at length and in detail each time this measure has come before the House of Commons during the last 13 years.
During the post-war years the drastic impact of mounting costs of production against the fixed and controlled price of gold has
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act operated with shattering effect upon the industry. In 1946 the Canadian gold production totalled only 2.8 million ounces as compared to 5.4 million ounces in 1941. The number of operating mines had been reduced from 140 to 88. Prospecting and exploration for new properties was brought to a standstill, and the towns and communities which depended on gold mining activity had suffered to the point where their future existence was in jeopardy.
The gravity of the situation was recognized at the time by the Canadian government, and assistance was afforded by the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which came into effect on January 1, 1948. As I have already mentioned, with a few modifications and amendments required to meet changing conditions the act has been periodically renewed. It is due to expire at the end of the current calendar year, and parliament is asked to extend the operation of the act to 1961, 1962 and 1963.
The enactment of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in 1948 was made in the light of the conditions existing then. It was not anticipated that during the ensuing years there would be as sharp a drop in the mint price of gold as we have experienced since 1955. When the act was amended in 1958 it provided a straight increase of 25 per cent. That increase was welcomed, but it could have been 50 per cent and it would not have been exaggerated. To prove my point here are some figures which will be of interest to the committee.
After 1948 the general trend of the Canadian mint price of gold as determined by the fluctuation of the Canadian-United States exchange rate was upward, rising from the $35 that it was then to $38.05 in 1950. From 1950 the trend was exactly the opposite; it dropped steadily during the following six years, and the average price per ounce during that period was $34.75. During the last three years, 1957, 1958 and 1959, the average price per ounce was $33.70, and not so very long ago it went down to $33.13 per ounce.
The average price per ounce of gold paid by the Royal Canadian Mint in the first quarter of 1960 was $33.22 compared with $33.54, the average for the whole of 1959, $33.98 in 1958, $33.55 in 1957, $34.45 in 1956 and $34.52 in 1955. This deterioration in the mint price for gold during the last three years had a tremendous effect on the industry, and the increase in subsidy in 1958 was more than justified. The average mint price per ounce of gold for that period, from 1948 to 1956 inclusive, was $35.40 while the average for the last three years, 1957, 1958 and 1959, was only $33.70. This represents a loss of $1.70.
4226	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
The gold mines eligible for federal assistance produced an estimated 8.2 million ounces during the last three years. The loss of $1.70 per ounce represents a loss of revenue to these mines of some $14.4 million. This of itself nullified 44 per cent of all the assistance received during that same period, which is estimated at about $33 million including the 25 per cent increase in 1958 and 1959. The gold mining industry has been caught in the squeeze of diminishing revenues and increased costs, and considering that condition it is not surprising that the number of producing gold mines has been reduced from 88 in 1946 to 50 in 1959.
Mr. Chairman, high tribute is paid by everyone in a position to judge to the consistent and remarkable efforts which the gold producers have made in achieving the maximum of efficiency and economy. The gold miners themselves and other employees in the Canadian gold mines have also brought their contribution to bear in this respect. In many ways production crews have fought successfully against the forces of inflation, and so have continued operations which could well have been expected to close.
Those men responsible for the continuing production in the 50 Canadian gold mines we now have in operation, including the executives, the managers, the hard rock miners, surface employees and others, should be given full credit for their resourcefulness, determination and good work.
The price of gold, however, fixed by the policy of governments and, as far as Canada is concerned, subject to fluctuation with the Canadian-United States rates of exchange, is something entirely beyond the power of the gold producers and their employees to control.
The conditions under which gold mines have had to operate have grown increasingly unfavourable and are much more difficult now than they were in 1948 when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was instituted.
It is not possible to record any easement of operating conditions since 1956. Costs have continued to climb, and only recently has there been evidence of some levelling out in the costs of supplies. Wages, which account for close to 60 per cent of operating costs, have of necessity been increased periodically since 1948. Also there has been further decline in the mint price of gold since 1956 and, as I mentioned earlier, the mint price went as low as $33.13 in November, 1959. Indeed, the decline in the mint price of gold during the last three years has been one of the most severe handicaps with which the industry has had to contend.


Under the double impact of reduced revenue and increased costs, the cost-price squeeze has brought most of the gold mines to a more highly critical condition than any experienced since the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was first instituted. This is why I said earlier in my remarks that the 25 per cent increase in subsidy in 1958 hardly compensated for increased costs since 1956, and that an increase of 50 per cent would have been more in line, especially in view of the adverse effect created by the high premium on the Canadian dollar which has prevailed during the last three years.
Fortunately, during the last month the premium on the Canadian dollar has come down substantially and this is of special significance to the hard-pressed gold mining industry. Yesterday the premium dropped to 1.3 per cent as compared to 4.27 per cent, the average for 1959. The Leader of the Opposition tells me that today the premium dropped to 1 per cent. So it can be seen that this drop to date represents an increase of more than $1 an ounce in the mint price for gold. If the Canadian dollar were to stabilize around par with the United States dollar the present formula of calculating the assistance paid to the gold mines would be just about right. On the other hand, if the present drop in the value of the Canadian dollar as compared to the United States dollar is only temporary, and if it is to go back to a high premium again, the present formula of calculating the assistance is certainly not adequate.
It is hardly necessary to emphasize that gold is a monetary metal and that it is un-dervaluated at $35 U.S. an ounce. The price of gold has not advanced with the rise in wages and the prices of commodities, with the result that the cost of producing gold in many of our Canadian mines is much higher than $35.
It is also a fact that the function and value of gold has been much played down during the post-war years. However, this trend seems to have been reversed lately, and it is encouraging to note the growing importance which is being attached by many prominent economists to greater production and availability of gold for the purpose of arriving at full convertibility of national currencies and promoting an increased volume of world trade.
A great number of monetary authorities consider an increase in the price of gold inevitable, but when will it come no one knows, and few will venture to guess. In the opinion of some economists, factors which might cause a change of attitude in United States include the threat of a major depression, or

a loss of gold to such an extent that United States reserves would drop to a very low level.
In the meantime the gold mining industry and the dependent communities of this country continue to be crushed between a declining price and rising costs. The answer to the question as to how many mines and communities will be able to survive and for how long depends on the wisdom of the Canadian government in continuing the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act on a fair and reasonable basis.
In introducing this resolution, the minister has mentioned certain changes in connection with the administration of the act. We will know more about those when we have the bill.
I would like the minister to give serious consideration to another minor amendment to the act, an amendment which would add very little to the total amount of assistance payable by the government but which would at the same time remove what I think has been an anomaly, more particularly since the government has deemed it advisable to increase the subsidy by 25 per cent.
Of all the gold mines operating in Canada and receiving assistance under the act there are a few with operating costs exceeding $45 per ounce. The maximum assistance to which these mines are entitled under the act is restricted in this way: that the rate of assistance factor is determined by taking two thirds of the amount by which the cost per ounce exceeds $26.50 with a maximum of $12.33. "With a maximum of $12.33" is the restrictive part of the formula. When it was deemed advisable to increase the subsidy by 25 per cent, this was done because the government and parliament were satisfied that increased production costs were such that an increase of subsidy was justified.
The anomaly is, according to me, that we are not using the same yardstick for those mines with costs exceeding $45 per ounce. For this reason I believe that the maximum of $12.33 should be increased. I leave this matter to the good judgment of the minister, and I hope he will give it full consideration.
Canada's annual gold production is approximately 4.5 million ounces of which 3.9 million are produced by lode gold mines and placer operations, and the remaining 600,000 ounces as a by-product of base metal mines. Of the 50 lode gold mines in production, all but nine qualify for assistance under the terms of the act, having annual costs in excess of $26.50 per ounce of gold produced. Few of these 41 mines could survive for any appreciable length of time without the assistance received through the Emergency Gold Mining Act.
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
To substantiate this I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the facts revealed in the following analysis:
1. Twenty four gold producers, producing 34 per cent of lode gold production from assisted mines, have operating costs in excess of the current mint price. Thirty two producers producing 75 per cent to 80 per cent of the lode gold production from assisted mines have costs in excess of $30 an ounce.
It is evident that mines in the first group would have little or no chance at all of survival in the absence of assistance. It is also evident that of the additional eight mines with costs between $30 and $34 an ounce few would be in a position to continue production either at all or for any length of time. Mine shut-downs in many parts of Canada would be inevitable and what is more serious, most of these shut-downs would be permanent.
The gold mining industry currently affords steady employment to more than 18,000 Canadians as compared to more than 20,000 in 1950. Most of these are the heads of families and support a number of dependants. In addition it is estimated that for each man employed in a gold mine four others are given employment in industries supplying the mines with goods and services.
Any further drastic curtailment in gold mining employment would have very serious effects on the general employment situation in Canada, which is not only less satisfactory now than it has been for many years, but is very critical. Only today the dominion bureau of statistics has reported that for the month of April there were 517,000 unemployed and seeking jobs, as compared to 445,000 for the same month in 1959. The effects, direct or indirect, of any substantial reduction in gold mining employment are bound to have serious repercussions on the national economy and would certainly require extensive and expensive measures of rehabilitation and relief.
No industry is satisfied to feel that it is in any measure dependent for its continued existence upon the federal treasury. On the other hand, no industry concurs willingly in its own demise. In considering the over-all cost to the Canadian government of expenditures made under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act there are a number of factors which are not to be overlooked. In the first place, even if the federal treasury had to pay some $131 million in assistance to the gold mines from 1948 to 1959 inclusive, it is important to note that the cost per ounce including the subsidy for all the gold purchased by the Canadian government during that period was only about 50 cents

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act above the average price per ounce the government had to pay during that period of 10 years previous to 1948.
Second, the government of Canada during the last 12 years has built up a substantial reserve of gold. As a result of even a moderate variation in the Canada-United States rate of exchange these stocks would show substantial appreciation. In the event of a revaluation of the price of gold the benefits which would accrue would more than compensate for all the expenditures made under E.G.M.A. and the Canadian government and the Canadian people will be the chief beneficiaries.
Third, we must not forget that a substantial portion of the amount paid in assistance returns to the federal treasury in the form of taxes. In these circumstances, the amounts paid out as assistance seem a very small price to pay for the advantages to be gained by maintaining strong gold reserves, by keeping alive the gold mining communities across the country which otherwise would become ghost towns and by maintaining high employment in these communities.

I did not pay too much attention to that part of the hon. member's remarks, but in addition to that he suggested that my speech was written by the gold mining industry or the association. The hon. member for Timmins well knows it is contrary to the rules
[Mr. Dumas.l
to impute, directly or indirectly, motives to any hon. member. subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION, ETC.
speechtext:
My reference was entirely to the material in the hon. member's speech. Since there are two sides to every story and as only one side has been presented so far by the hon. member, before presenting the other side of the story I should like to fill in a few points which the hon. member missed in regard to the difficult position in which the gold mining industry finds itself.
I have here a list of the most essential materials used in the gold mining industry such as timber, posts lagging, cribbing timber, steel plate, grinding balls, powder, cyanide and so forth. The costs of these commodities increased between 1945 and 1959. As has already been pointed out the fluctuations of the Canadian dollar make a difference and these figures may not apply as of this date but as of the end of 1959 the price received by the industry dropped to 86 per cent of what it was in 1945. The cost of essential materials used in the industry, on the other hand, increased in this period. British Columbia fir square timber increased in cost to 281 per cent; spruce 2 x 4's increased in price to 160 per cent; the cost of 2 x 8's increased to 179 per cent; the cost of 9-inch round posts increased to 211 per cent; the cost of lagging increased to 212.5 per cent; the cost of cribbing timber increased to 200 per cent. And so on down the line; the smallest increase shown in any major product used in this industry was in that of cyanide, which increased to only 129 per cent.
There is a good side and a bad side to everything, Mr. Chairman. To get a proper picture of any problem you have to look at both sides. The picture painted of the gold mining industry has been that of the great big brother or father, or what have you. We have been told that, if given the opportunity, this industry was going to do so much for the employees and the communities in which the employees live. I do not think that is giving the proper picture. Certainly, it is not one substantiated by the history of this industry. I think we need no better illustration than to go back to 1934 or 1935 when the increase in the price of gold came into effect, when gold jumped from $20 an ounce to $35 an ounce, an increase of 75 per cent. At that time the employees received the grand sum of 5 cents an hour as an increase.

There is another factor, too, that we must keep in mind if we are going to have a fair and reasonable view of this problem. While it is true that there is a fixed price for the product of the gold mining industry and while costs keep going up the price stays the same or, if the exchange on the dollar happens to go the wrong way, the price can even decrease, yet the fact still remains that it is the only industry in this country which knows exactly what it is going to get for every ounce of product that it produces. In that respect at least it is placed in a more favourable position than some of the other industries.
It has been mentioned on one or two occasions today that the purpose of this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was to help the industry. Certainly history has shown us that that is exactly what has happened but, I think, if we look at the original act and read the preamble to it we will find that the original intention was to help the gold mining communities and to prevent them from becoming ghost towns. There are a couple of ways in which that could be done. There is one temporary way in which it could be done and that is by paying straight assistance to the industry to keep it going, to lengthen its life. But again we must keep something in mind. The day of reckoning must come because gold is a wasting asset. Whether we extend the operation 5, 10 or 50 years, the day is going to come when there will be no more gold in those mines. Then what will happen to the communities? Therefore, there are two ways in which this very commendable objective can be reached. One is, as we have been doing in the past 12 years, to pay a subsidy directly to the industry with no strings attached.
I should like hon. members to answer one question. Are we any closer today to solving the problem of the gold mining communities than we were 12 years ago before this $131 million had been paid from the public treasury. I maintain that we are not. If the Hollinger and McIntyre mines in Timmins were to close tomorrow we would have another Matachewan ghost town on our hands, only a much bigger one. We are not one step closer to solving the problem of the communities than we were in 1948.
How much value have we had for this $131 million that we have spent from the public treasury? I do not think anyone really knows. That is why on every possible occasion since I came down here in 1957-and the hon. member for Timiskaming has also endeavoured to do the same on many occasions -I have tried to get this government to establish a committee consisting of the five
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act interested parties, namely the federal government which pays the subsidy, the provincial government which administers the mining act, the municipalities which are so directly involved, the industry as represented by the gold operators and the miners and employees as represented by their trade unions, and have this committee look into all aspects of the gold mining industry to see if in fact we are getting value for our money, or whether there is some much better way in which this money can be spent in the future.
When we take into account the public at large, the gold mining communities, the investments in those communities, the capital investments, the houses, the schools, the churches, the streets, the sewers, the sidewalks, what are we going to have in those gold mining communities across the country 25 years from now? Will we have 50 ghost towns and 100 years from now 300 ghost towns, or is there some other way in which some use can be made of this capital investment, some better way than the one we have at the present time?
On other occasions I have listed some of the reasons why we cannot be too sympathetic toward some of the gold operators whom we have in this country at the present time. I am sorry to report that the conditions I have listed on more than one occasion have not improved. As time has gone by the gold operators of this country have not changed, they are just as unreasonable today as they were two years, five years and ten years ago. In the gold mining industry they are still fighting the battle that was fought in every other industry 25, 50 and 100 years ago. We are still being paid very low wages in the gold mining industry today. I know the mines are pleading poverty, and especially right at the present time when negotiations are opening up for a new contract. If you talk to many of the gold mining people up in my area they will tell you it looks as if the mine is going to close down this year and everybody is going to be out of work, and if you talk to someone else you find that negotiations have opened up and you know this talk will go on until a contract is signed and you will hear no more about the mine closing until the contract is opened up again.
Over the past four or five years we have seen another practice develop in the gold mining industry. As soon as the mines first opened up in Elliott Lake, at Bancroft and at Manitouwadge, and so on, where wages were twice what they were in the gold mining industry, the top miners started to trickle away from the gold mines. I do not think one could blame them too much when the wages in the Timmins area, for example, ran from $1.25

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to $1.50 an hour and in the Elliot Lake area they were in the neighbourhood of $3.00 an hour.
Instead of trying to compete and trying to increase wages sufficiently to keep these people at home with their families and in houses they have built and paid for-these people did not want to leave the community; their roots were very deep in the community and many of them were born there-the gold mining industry established the practice of sending recruiting teams over to Britain and Europe to bring in immigrants to replace the men. Those immigrants, or many of them, stayed only long enough to pay back their fare; and, if they did not know the French or English language, long enough to learn enough of the language to enable them to move to another place, and the gold mining industry and the gold mining communities became a sort of training ground for immigrants.
This practice is still being continued. Even in the face of the present mining situation, with which we are all familiar, with uranium mines closing down all over the place and experienced miners returning to the gold fields, what do they find? They find that two mines in the Timmins area, Hollinger Consolidated Gold Mines and McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited, the two biggest operators in the Timmins camp, have recruiting teams over in Britain trying to lure men to come over and get these jobs ahead of the returning miners.
There was some controversy over this not too long ago. I was talking one day to the personnel manager of Hollinger Mines, and he told me that these reports were not in accordance with the facts, and that when the figures were published showing the number of miners the company had rehired, somebody's face would be very red. I wrote him a letter a while ago, and I should like to quote a portion of that letter today. I said:
-but I would like to have discussed this recent problem that has arisen relative to immigrants versus local miners.
As I stated in the house when speaking on this subject on Friday last-
This letter is dated February 29, 1960.
-I have seen arguments both pro and con in our newspapers, and I am not in a position at the present time to say who is right and who is wrong. However, I do know of two particular cases which caused me considerable concern. If there are any reasons why these two men should not be hired I would like to know, if only for my personal and confidential information. One, of course, I have already discussed with you, Mr. Leo Gagnon. In fact I might say it was my understanding that that matter was settled when I first came down at the opening of this session. I have been told since that he went down to the Hollinger on Monday morning and received the same answer he had received previously "They would keep him in mind".

The other case is one involving Mr. Leo Lepine, who at the present time lives at 142 Dome avenue, South Porcupine, who according to the information I have, has been given what is commonly known as the run-around. He has six years mining experience, and he is only 36 years of age and is supposed to be a first class miner.
As I said previously, if there are reasons why these men should not be hired I have never been told. I would appreciate any light you can throw on this subject.
When I did not receive an answer to this letter I wrote again on March 28, 1960 and I said:
On checking my files I failed to find an answer to my letter of February 29.
Would you be kind enough to forward me another copy.
Needless to say, I have still to receive an answer to this letter. In the light of this fact I can only assume, Mr. Chairman, that these charges that we read in our newspapers are true. I know of cases where immigrants have been hired at the Hollinger mine when their only previous experience was that of store clerk or, in one case, an instructor at a technical school.
I should like to point out that our Minister of Labour has certainly had an embarrassing time this session in trying to solve all the unemployment problems. A situation such as this tends to confuse the unemployment issue and further embarrass the minister. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration cannot escape scot-free in this instance because immigration, whether it comes directly through her office or-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the present time this committee is being asked to renew the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I would suggest that before the committee can come to a proper decision as to whether or not this act should be renewed, it should have as clear a picture as it is possible to have of the gold mining industry and its ramifications. This is the purpose of my remarks.
Another thing of which this committee should take full cognizance is the fact that these same companies I mentioned before, Hollinger Consolidated Gold Mines and McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited, have from the year 1948 and up to March 1, 1959- another year has been added since I obtained these figures-received the following amounts under this act: Hollinger had received a total of $9,271,488.50 and McIntyre had received $5,704,781.82. During the 12 years which they were receiving that money, this total of over $15 million from the Canadian taxpayers, the

Hollinger opened up the huge Ungava iron ore empire in Labrador and McIntyre is reported to have bought out Algoma Steel, the estate of the late Sir James Dunn in Sault Ste Marie.
Current rumour is that negotiation are under way now for a merger between these two mines. They are located adjacent to each other, one on each side of the highway. McIntyre recently had a large copper strike. I am told that they have 12 million tons of copper mapped out. The purpose of these negotiations would be to mill all the gold from McIntyre in the Hollinger mill and turn McIntyre into a copper mill, yet retain its identity as a gold mine so that the company could receive the gold subsidy.
These are some of the things that this committee could ascertain. These are some of the things that this committee should know before passing legislation of this kind. Are we getting value for our money? Are we spending it sensibly and in the best way we can or are a few smart operators putting it over the Canadian public There is no question in my mind but that many of the gold mines operating today would not be operating were it not for this act. In the main, I would say this is a good act and is one that has been very beneficial, particularly to my region of northern Ontario.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act makes provision for inspectors to visit these mines to make sure that everything is as it should be. After considerable difficulty last year we discovered that not only had these mines never been inspected by a government inspector, but that there was no such person on the payroll. How do we know that everything is in order?
I would say, that one thing that should be given very prompt and very careful consideration is the matter of establishing secondary industries in our mining towns. We do not have to look any further than the recent disastrous effect of the drop in the market for uranium to see what the results can be for a town whose economy is based on mining. We have seen a modern city like Elliot Lake facing the possibility, unless something new is developed, of becoming a ghost town. The only difference between Elliot Lake and practically all the gold mining communities is that in the case of Elliot Lake this development only took five years, whereas in the case of the gold mining communities it may take 20, 40 or 100 years. The end result will be exactly the same.
I would say, Mr. Chairman, that this is a very urgent problem. If these communities are going to continue, then the government must renew this act. However, I repeat that in its
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act present form it does not appear to be the answer. I say it is a simple matter for this government to get the knowledge that is required. We have been paying out for 12 years now at the rate of $12 million a year to accomplish a certain purpose. Are we accomplishing that purpose or is there a much better way of spending this money?

I believe that the mining industry in Canada deserves every commendation on the part of Canadian citizens and of this government. I think any industry which has not only been able to survive but to increase its efficiency to the peak it has now attained, with some 18,000 employees, deserves a great deal of credit.
Under this particular act it is proposed to spend, I understand, something like $12 million a year in order to make sure that 18,000 employees still maintain their jobs. Of course there are other incidental benefits, extremely important as they may be, but the fact is that this government is going to continue to spend $12 million a year in order to keep 18,000 employees at work.
The gold mining industry itself has done a great deal to help itself. This recent action to permit the sale of gold bars, the question of having listed the one kilogram gold bar on the Toronto stock exchange and the increase in the purchase of gold bars in this country are making many people realize the important part that only gold can play in reflecting and keeping sound values in our dollar.
Furthermore, the export of gold is increasing in most countries of the world. Close to 6 per cent of the total United States reserves of gold went out of the United States in 1959; that is more than $1 billion worth. I feel, of course, that gold should and must be an export item. I think our government would be well advised to continue and to increase the efforts which it has been expending to promote the export of gold throughout the world.
The fact that the United States exported $1 billion of its reserves of gold in 1959 means that the United States has diminishing reserves of gold and is to some extent losing the freedom of movement in its fiscal position with regard to gold. The United States government either must raise the price of gold or run the risk of slackening all the more the gold standard which has fairly well been discarded.
I should like to present what I feel are one or two important problems. According to the information I am able to get through the dominion bureau of statistics, the Bank of Canada has in its reserves $1,800 million. Of this amount only $1 billion is represented in gold, the other $800 million being represented in long term and short term United
4232	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act States securities and United States dollars. I feel that this government should give serious consideration to using gold for a large portion of the $800 million that is now represented in United States currency which in itself has not the value possessed by the Canadian gold reserves, dollarwise, nor are those values likely to equate themselves over the next few years.
We have the fact that gold mining is a very important industry, that the export of gold is being more and more practised by many countries, that the gold reserves of the Bank of Canada could be much greater, and also that world trade in the past 20 years has developed more than six times as fast as have the gold reserves of the free world. For all these reasons and many more which I will not mention this afternoon I feel that a thorough investigation should be made by means of a royal commission appointed to study the effect of subsidies with regard to all our mining activities.
As the Minister of Veterans Affairs will be able to point out, we have in eastern New Brunswick recently discovered minerals and mines that warrent development; but unless something is done to guarantee the prices and to encourage these industries to develop these mines, I greatly doubt whether those mines will be developed for many years to come.
I feel that the whole problem of the mining industry in Canada, not only with regard to gold but with regard to all other metals, should receive the serious consideration and the studies which a royal commission could provide. I am not trying to belittle the gold mining industry nor am I trying to give any impression that I am not wholeheartedly behind this resolution. However, I feel that this resolution in itself is not much more than a stopgap measure and that some serious thought and study should go into the problem of solving our mining problems in this country.

The first job I was given when I went to work in a gold mine was one that was most unpopular of all. It is called mucking out the sump. You have to get down in the drip and dirt, mucking over the boot, to keep it clear from all the things that come down the shaft. The unfortunate thing about mucking out is that it is a job that must always be carried on on a fairly regular basis. Otherwise the shaft fills up and the mine cannot work. It seems to me that the minister is performing the function today, through this resolution, of mucking out the sumps of the gold mining industry in the main. It is a task that must be done.


We have already had from a number of hon. members arguments that indicate that this legislation is no solution in itself. I want to speak about several aspects of the problem, one of which is something that has been touched on slightly by the hon. member for Timmins and to which I have directed the attention of the minister on previous occasions. I can make the point just as well to start with by reading a quotation from an article in the Toronto Star of last spring, wherein it was stated:
Criticism by C.C.F. member of parliament Douglas Fisher that the government hands out millions of dollars in cost-aid to gold mines with inadequate inspection of the mines is ill-founded, the two mining organizations commented.
That is the Canadian Metal Mining Association for one and the Ontario mining association for the other. The article continues:
"It is a pure cost inspection-the inspectors don't have to go underground," said Mr. Wansborough.
He is managing director of this association.
He said Mr. Fisher had confused the functions of a provincial mine inspector, who checks to see safe mining practices are used, and a federal inspector.
No mining company ever thought the cost-aid examination of a mine's accounts and records was lax, he said.
The mistake in this interpretation by Mr. Wansborough is that I was mistaken and mixed up the provincial and the federal functions. I think we have enough examples- I would mention the Jacques Cartier bridge situation-to make us realize that wherever the federal government is receiving or paying out revenue it is our duty to be suspicious of human nature and that we have to make sure about the safety of the funds the government is receiving and paying out.
I want to point out to the minister one matter. I do not know whether or not he will be introducing an amendment, but I should like to point out to him that in the original act-and I believe the situation still exists-which is chapter 95 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, section 6, provides as follows:
6. The Minister may, as a condition to the making of any payment to a person under this Act, require that person
(a) to permit any person authorized by the Minister in that behalf, at any reasonable time, to enter upon and examine the mine from which the gold in respect of which the payment is to be made is produced, and all works and premises in connection therewith and to have access to and to examine all books and records of that person relating to the production of gold from the mine and the cost of production thereof during any period relevant for the purposes of this Act,-
I would like the minister to explain to me how he can leave that wording in the act

when spokesmen for the mining organizations say that some kind of underground inspection is necessary.
No one wants to throw harpoons just for the sake of harpooning the mining industry, but we all know the reputation that certain segments of the industry have for its stock promotion practices and other kind of deals. We know the reputation that sort of thing has on the security exchanges in the United States. It seems to me that the minister and his department are far too bland in paying out this immense sum now totalling over $130 million without going underground and examining the workings of the mines, especially in view of the fact that every miner I have talked to, in the main not educated men but skilled in their trade, in a gold mine receiving emergency gold mining assistance has always indicated that he believes from his knowledge, admittedly not technical or scientific, that low grading is going on.
In the face of this kind of argument, which may be a completely blind and stupid accusation, how the minister can go along without bothering to make the kind of inspection necessary is beyond me. We are paying out all this money. These mining promoters are always depicting themselves as great entrepreneurs, and they have done their share in that regard. But despite that, why should we accept these people when they are not making the kind of check and scrutiny they should make by going down underground and looking at their workings to make sure they are mining the mine in a way that they are not taking advantage of the government purse.
We have so many examples today where the government is handing out aid in various directions. There is the industry which I think the hon. member for Villeneuve spoke of and I think he will admit there has been a remarkable consolidation in the last ten years where more and more of these smaller prospects have been drawn into what you might call large corporate structures. I think of the Little Long Lac situation as an example of the way a group of people using one corporate organization have moved out and brought a whole bunch of other mines within their structure.
One of the obvious things one notes about any kind of tax deal today, especially a tax situation where mines in the first three years of their life are exempt from certain taxation imposts, is that we know that by consolidation of a going concern with one which is not going you can get certain tax deterioration allowances. That should make the government suspicious and I think rightly and
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act justly suspicious. Why should we not be suspicious where money is involved, no matter what person or organization is concerned? Yet here there is a situation where a section is put into the act allowing underground inspection and the minister admits it is never carried out; all we have is an examination by a cost accountant. Probably there is no mine in Canada where there is any tomfoolery going on, but I believe we have every right to expect the minister to be suspicious of them all and to take the steps implied by the act to make sure we are not giving money to mines which do not deserve it. I would certainly be interested to know whether the minister would consider receiving any amendments that would cut out this portion of section 6 of the act, if this section is of no use at all.
I was interested in another point which was brought up by some people who correspond with me, namely the position of the shareholders of a number of these companies that take advantage of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. These companies take advantage of the act and yet never pay dividends; at least, many of them have never paid dividends since they became involved in these corporate consolidations. Again the great example here is Little Long Lac.
A shareholder today theoretically has a form of democratic control in that as a shareholder he can go to a meeting and make his point. But we all know that in effect in most corporate organizations today you have to be a very major shareholder to have any influence in this kind of situation. I think the minister will admit that there is hardly a gold mine today receiving cost statements or benefits from the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act where the little shareholder would really have any voice at all. More and more we get the situation where giants such as Hollinger, McIntyre, Rio Tinto and No-randa hold big blocks of shares in many of these smaller mines.
What position does this leave the smaller shareholder in, especially when looking at a company like Little Long Lac which is receiving emergency gold mining assistance through some of its subsidiaries? Some of these mines which have come under Little Long Lac control which once paid dividends are not paying them now despite the fact that they are getting more emergency gold mining assistance.
It seems to me that this example should point out reasons for being suspicious of the gold mining people. I do not say we should be any more suspicious of them than of anyone else who takes something from the public purse; but I certainly feel that if the minister

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act does not want to carry out or have his officials carry out the purpose of section 6 as set out in the act, and that if all the gold mines need is merely a cost inspection, he should let us know and we should wipe this part of the section out of the act. Why is it in there if a genuine inspection of the mine workings is not necessary? What is the contingency that keeps it on the books? I insist that the minister should be suspicious of everyone who receives funds from the federal treasury and suspicious to the extent of making absolutely sure there is no question of the integrity of the operation producing the figures which the minister's accountant goes to see.
I can certainly see situations arising every year where scandals brew up because it is apparent that the federal government and the provincial government concerned have not taken proper precautions to see that these scandals should not happen. How can the minister give an assurance when from the figures he has given us he is not carrying out what the act allows him to do? He says it is completely unnecessary. I think if the minister has that much faith in the gold mines and says that all you need is this cost inspection, then we should wipe that part of the section out of the act because it really serves no purpose at all.
Mr. Chairman, one point the hon. member for Timmins touched on-and this is the old refrain

was this. What is the long term solution to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act? Many of these mines are going out of production. We see examples in the Red Lake mine field which are quite heartening. I understand from the hon. member who represents that area that only one mine is now receiving assistance.
All of them at one time.

The hon. member interjects and says that at one time all of them were. But we must give them credit for their technical abilities and the money they have poured in. They have gone deeper and opened up new zones, and Red Lake is much more a going camp. But you still have the situation, especially in a community like Timmins, where the whole life of the region is based on something which has this very shaky basis of emergency gold mine assistance. I certainly feel that we have not only the right but the duty to call for some long term measure. I think that is what the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska was suggesting, that we have to have some long term way of treating this gold mining situation.
The hon. member for Villeneuve speculated on the financial effects of the move of the

United States dollar to parity with the Canadian dollar. What is to be the situation if this trend towards parity keeps right on going past the even mark, and the Canadian dollar is at a discount to the United States dollar? Obviously certain sections of our industry would be overjoyed, because that would mean a real benefit to the pulp and paper industry, the shipping industry, the gold mining industry and the base metal industry. But what would be the effects in relation to this particular act? After all, this assistance is set up on a certain scale to assist mines in accordance with some kind of ratio or formula. If the United States dollar continues at a discount of three or four cents compared with the Canadian dollar-and this seems feasible in view of the shift which has taken place in the last two weeks-what adjustment does the minister contemplate, if any, in relation to the amount of assistance provided for the gold mines? I think we would be glad to hear from the minister on that score.
If the minister has already given the information, well and good, but as the hon. member for Villeneuve pointed out, the recent move in exchange rates is an asset to the gold mining industry. But if the trend continues, it is surely a case where the government might consider pulling in its horns and spending less money on emergency gold mining assistance. I should like to hear the minister's views on that situation. We must remember in connection with interest rates or anything of that kind that there are shifts and changes, and here we have a portent of a very significant shift which, I think, will be beneficial in the main but is it going to be beneficial to the taxpayers who are putting up this money?
I have in effect asked a number of questions of the minister, and I hope that later on when we have the bill before us we will have an opportunity of hearing from him on these points especially on the point raised in connection with section 6 and the provision which permits inspection of the workings of a mine. I would also like to have an explanation from the minister as to the technical problems involved. After all, as one who has worked underground, I know it is not easy to appreciate all that goes on in a mine unless you have bad news from a whole host of places. The factors are complicated, and I wonder if the minister is in the position of having staff who can carry out inspections of the actual workings of a mine which would confirm the audit he seems prepared to accept.
[Mr. Fisher.j

Perhaps I might make a few brief remarks before this resoiution is passed. We have been asked to approve a resolution to extend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to cover the years 1961, 1962 and 1963.
I listened a few moments ago to the remarks made by the hon. member for Timmins. He referred to the fact that if this action were not taken by the government, ghost towns would replace the communities where gold mining is at present carried on. The present situation results from the good measures which were taken by the previous administration in order to prevent ghost towns replacing mining communities. I think this action should be set up as an example and as guidance to the present government especially so far as Springhill, Nova Scotia is concerned and particularly with regard to Elliot Lake, of which we have heard so much in this house in recent times.
The hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska referred to mining developments in northern New Brunswick. We all know that we have in northern New Brunswick one of the largest base metal potentials in Canada. Yet these deposits in the Bathurst area are receiving no attention whatever from the government. The only time we hear about them is when there is a federal or provincial election when there are indications that the mines will be reopened and that everything will be all right. That is what is happening in New Brunswick at the present time. I would urge the government to give our mining area the attention it deserves.
The manager of the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company in an address at Bathurst a few days ago said the company will succeed in bringing those mines into production, but only after hard struggle and sweat. This is a case where the government should take into consideration the importance for the area of the development of these minerals. Instead of devoting its attention to this northern vision-and I am not against the development of the north-I think we should give first attention to areas which are already inhabited and where we have potentials such as exist in northern New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Representing, as I do, one of the largest gold mining areas in Canada, I should be remiss if I did not take some part in the discussion of this particular resolution. I should like to make it very clearly understood that I am in favour of the extension of the provision of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and that I consider its extension necessary to the very life of the mining industry in my area.

Having said this, I should like to point out some of the things that are wrong with the act and suggest reasons why it does not serve the industry in the way which I think the originators of this act probably had in mind when they put it into effect. The mining industries of Canada, not only the gold mines but others, are always facing one problem or other. We have seen the gold mining industry facing problems that are very similar in their nature to the problems that are facing the mining communities of Elliot Lake, Bancroft and Uranium City. If you travel in the maritime provinces you will find that the problem in Springhill is no different from that which existed in Timmins and Kirkland Lake many years ago. This has been a perennial problem, not only in the gold mining industry but in the silver mining industry in my part of the country. Close to the turn of the century we saw the silver industry boom and bust, then repeat the process. People have waited for years and years for the day when silver would again reach a price at which the mines could be profitably operated. In this industry, without the benefit of any government assistance or government intervention, we have seen communities die and the people leave, and only those who are very hardy or very stubborn stay on. Then the time comes when the price of silver goes up again. The mines are relocated, and the industry goes on.
As a result of watching this process I have been interested in the long term results which have flowed from the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Act. I believe, as the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska said, that this was originally intended to be only a temporary measure. I am sure that members of parliament at that time were looking for a temporary and immediate solution to a problem with which they were faced in those years. Now, however, I think the time has come when the minister should amend the resolution before us in such a way as to take out the emergency part of the act, because it seeems to me that we are no closer to solving the problems in the gold mining industry today than we were when this act was first put into effect. If the act has accomplished what it was designed to let us make this assistance a permanent thing. The emergency aspect should be removed from the act and it could be made a regular subsidy.
If this were done other considerations would arise. If this method is satisfactory we could supply emergency assistance to other mining communities and make it possible to operate the mines and maintain the municipalities dependent on them. If the method is

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act satisfactory let us apply it to uranium and have a uranium mining emergency assistance act which would solve problems such as those in Elliot Lake. This is not quite as ridiculous as it sounds-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have talked to the people at Elliot Lake. They want the mines there to continue operating. We could stockpile uranium. The people of Elliot Lake do not care whether or not the product is sold immediately. I am sure that the hon. member for Gloucester would also urge that this assistance be extended to coal mining and the subventions could be removed.
If the act were extended in this form Canadians would be assured that the money was well spent in accomplishing what it was intended to. When the bill comes before us we should remove the words "emergency assistance".
I do not think this legislation accomplished what it was hoped it would accomplish. Gold mining areas cannot compete with the wages paid in other mining communities. Gold mining towns are reluctant and unable to improve services because of the tax structure. They have been unable to attract secondary industries. When the legislation was enacted I am sure it was intended not only to assist and maintain gold mining communities but to aid in the shift in dependence on the part of the communities from gold mining to secondary industry. It is more important than ever before that we now give close consideration to what the act should accomplish.
In the future demands from mining companies to stay in business will increase. Emergency assistance will be requested by the mining industries as it was by the gold mining industry in the days when it petitioned parliament for assistance. Would it not be reasonable for the uranium industry to ask for a subsidy to carry it over a temporary period during which the world demand for uranium does not equal the available supply? In perhaps 12 or 15 years I am convinced that the demand for uranium will tax the facilities of the industry. If successful, this act could be extended to Elliot Lake and other mining communities.
The other day when the Minister of Trade and Commerce stood up and said-

speechtext:
A few years ago the Ontario legislature set up a committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Knox a professor at Queen's University to investigate the gold mining industry to which committee many Ontario organizations presented briefs. The united steelworkers of America representing many gold mining employees pointed out that there are alternatives to E.M.G.A. Some of these proposals were published at the time of the publication of the committee's report. One alternative mentioned was that of increasing the price of gold. That was not possible at that time but the alternative becomes increasingly possible through the change in the value of the Canadian dollar and its relationship to the United States dollar. The union also recommended that the government press on the international market for an increase in the price of gold through the international monetary fund. The present Minister of Finance expressed himself as being in favour of this proposal before assuming his portfolio but has not mentioned the matter since. The union also pointed out that there were other ways of subsidizing the industry through giving consideration to a reduction in the taxes payable to the municipalities. The second one which is evident throughout the whole mining industry is the wages paid to the workers in the industry.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Chairman, we are interested in the maintenance and continuation of this subsidy. I agree with the hon. member for Timmins that other hon. members in the house have continually given the views of the mining industry. There is nothing wrong with that. I worked in the industry for 15 years and negotiated and bargained with the industry. From my experience with the industry's point of view, conditions that would satisfy the industry are not necessarily in the best interests of either the community or of the workers in the industry. Not always are the two interests analogous.
It seems to me that when we first set up this emergency gold mining assistance what we had in mind was that we were going to solve the problems of the community and of those people in the community who were dependent on mining the natural resources of the country. This is what we will have in mind when we attempt to solve the problems of the uranium mines. This is a case where we have let companies come

into an area and develop the natural resources of that area, but we have exercised very little control over them. In the gold mining industry we have never insisted that they put away a small amount of depreciation for their workers in their later life. We have never given any indication that we want them to take part of the contribution we make in the form of emergency gold mine assistance and place it into funds for the retirement of workers. We have not made payments of emergency gold mining assistance contingent on the development of secondary industries and the financing of those industries in the gold mining com-munites. It is with this thought in mind that I draw the minister's attention to this part of the program. It would be advantageous to eliminate the word "emergency" and just call the legislation "gold mining assistance act". The subsidy would be paid on a continuous basis and we should see that secondary industry is brought into the mining communities.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Timmins that the town of Timmins and its people are no farther along the road to developing secondary industries to take over when the gold mining industry is finished than it was years ago. Gold mining would have been finished and those communities would have been ghost towns now if it had not been for the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The day the mines are finished the camp is going to be in exactly the same position that it was in when the emergency gold mining assistance was brought into being. The communities are going to be left dependent on an industry which no longer exists. It would not exist today if it were not for this emergency assistance because the price of the product is not sufficient to carry the industry. It will be non-existant in the future because there will be no industry left. It seems to me one of our prime concerns should be to develop other industries and to look toward the day when the industry is no longer able to carry on and to provide for the community because the mines will have been worked out.

The minister will recall that I sent him instances of two or three stopes in a particular mine which I had been informed had been closed up and had been closed up for some time. In those stopes gold was running at several thousand dollars a ton, but never more than a few tons had been removed from them, and then only to maintain a certain grade from the mine. I will not argue with those who say this is good housekeeping. Maybe it is; maybe that is the way you should operate a mine, but I think those conditions exist to a great extent. If there were a large number of those particular stopes I am sure we would want to have inspectors there to see that the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act were complied with and that the figures presented to the auditors of the Department of Finance and the treasury authorities were such as to indicate the actual physical conditions available underground which could be ascertained from the books.
I have worked in enough different types of stopes to know that you cannot go down a mine and take a look at the face and estimate how the ore will run. This can only be done by a physical assay. When the mines themselves find that the amount of gold being extracted from ore is not in keeping with what their underground reports indicate they recheck and find out where the mistakes are and that is the only way it can be done. It can only be done by an examination of the reserves and the value of those reserves.
I am not prepared to debate which mines are high grading and which mines are low grading; I think there are mines doing both and I think it can be successfully argued by the mines that this may be good housekeeping and it may be the best way of operating the mines. They may be able to tell me and others, as the Northern Miner would indicate, that this is in the best interests of the people of Canada; but I suggest, Mr. Chairman, if we are to pay subsidies to them it may be in the best interests of the people who own and operate the particular mine but it may not be in the best interests of the mine itself.

I agree with the hon. member for Port Arthur that if this section of the act is not going to be complied with, if it is not going to be given any consideration, then we should remove it and take away the threat of an inspection at some time because, to the best of my knowledge-the minister can correct me if I am wrong-there are no inspectors in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys who have ever done any inspection underground; they have never done any sampling or made any tests in connection with emergency gold mining assistance or checked any particular mine in this respect.
There would not seem to be much point in bringing particular cases to the attention of the department if they have nobody to check on them. I have many friends who have worked many years in some of those particular mines who know the stopes. When you have worked in one particular stope and have worked there for two or three years every working day of those years it is not too difficult to recall the value at which the stope was running and the reasons why it was closed down. If a stope runs at $1,000 or $2,000 per ton, then I am quite sure a miner will remember that, just as he would remember if that stope were only running at $5 of $6 a ton and he was in danger of being moved out of that stope every time the company took a sample.
Those are the considerations that I believe must be kept in mind. I am going to trespass a little on your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but it seems to me we are going to be looking toward this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act more and more in the next few months or the next few years to ascertain whether or not it has done the job for the communities and for the people it was supposed to do. We shall be looking at what has been accomplished under this act in connection with other minerals as well as gold. If we find that the act has served the needs of the people it was meant to serve, then I think it has done so very cheaply.
However, Mr. Chairman, I believe that when we look at the basic problems this act was supposed to solve we will find it has done nothing to correct them. These basic problems will eventually have to be faced. One of these problems will be turning those communities that are dependent upon a primary industry into communities which have secondary industries. I would strongly suggest that we give consideration to amending this act to permit part of the money to be paid to subsidize other industries to go into the gold mining communities. Think what it would mean if we could give secondary industries the opportunity to come in and instead of
[Mr. Peters.1
paying $12 million in the form of gold mining assistance we could pay that amount in subsidies for secondary industries.
I suggest that these industries would not even have to consider the effect of such items as three years free taxes, communities already established, an existing labour force and municipal considerations such as sewers, water and other things. If we gave this $12 million and divided it up amongst the industries it would go a long way and you would see industries leaving Toronto overnight. This might be a much better long term solution to the problem of the mining industry than the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been. However, while we are giving this form of assistance I should like to see the government set up a new branch that would engage in planning for our natural resources so that we could get a much better distribution of our money and a much better distribution of industry. In this way we would not have the problems we have to face with this particular act, and our problems might be solved in a much better manner.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I might say that the people of northern Ontario are completely dependent upon this emergency gold mining assistance for their livelihood. They need it. They would like it increased. They would like the act made a permanent feature of government policy so that they could make plans. I would suggest that many of the mines, particularly the small ones such as the one in which I worked in Timmins for many years, do give consideration to their employees. The small mine in which I worked was concerned with the conservation of the mine and worked very hard in an effort to get as much life out of that mine as it was possible to do. This has not been true of some of the other mines which I have had the opportunity of examining over the years. Many of them were more interested in piling up dividends than they were in conserving the mineral and extending the life of the mine. They were much more interested in buying steel companies and other things, and in this way they did not serve the needs of the communities in the way this act provided. They served the needs of the few, as the hon. member for Port Arthur indicated, by gobbling up these little mines that were not quite able to look after themselves.
I hope that the minister will give some consideration to these problems. They are very real problems in northern Ontario. If he did not believe that this act was serving the needs of the communities and the people dependent on this industry, then I am quite sure he would not have asked for the extension of this act. However, he has seen fit to

ask for this extension and I hope he will give some consideration to making it more successful in extending the life of our communities.

We have to pay these subsidies because those are institutions serving the public interest as a whole. Those are institutions which, apparently, are unable to survive otherwise and we need them.
