The hon. member for Port Arthur spoke about the United States dollar. The hon. member for Port Arthur, who I see is now back in the committee, mentioned the matter of low grading. This is not the first time the matter has been brought up in the house. I see from Hansard that every year a member of the C.C.F. party speaks about the low grading question. I will give him my answer again and will be as patient as he is in putting his question.
The subject of low grading has been raised on previous occasions and it would appear that it is not yet appreciated that the practice is a highly improbable one for practical reasons. Perhaps the most important of these reasons is that a deliberate reduction in the grade of ore milled by a gold mine operator for the purpose of increasing the amount of assistance payable to him is a highly unprofitable move. The reduced amount of gold produced in such a case results in a greater loss of revenue from the sale of gold than is represented by the increase in the amount of assistance payable. This view of the matter is substantiated by the fact that there were 13 gold mines in Canada in 1959 which were not eligible for assistance payments under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for the sole reason that their cost of production was less than $26.50 per ounce. If low grading is as profitable as the hon. member appears to think, it would be logical for these mines to reduce the grade of ore milled to the point where their costs would be greater than $26.50 per ounce and so become eligible for assistance. The fact that they have not done so

I think that would be the simplest way out of it and if we were satisfied it would probably end our discussion of the matter.

Would the minister give an answer to this question. Everyone who has spoken has agreed that the act is both good and necessary but there are always those who seek to abuse these things and that is what is bothering me, other hon. members of the committee and many engaged in the gold mining industry. Without an opportunity to examine the inspectors I believe the fear in the minds of the people will increase.
Is the minister giving any consideration to the suggestion I made earlier today with regard to establishing a committee comprising federal, provincial and municipal representatives, representatives of the mining authorities and union representatives of the employees in order to look into the matter and allay the fears expressed today.

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection at all to considering this proposal.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF SALE OF FEEDS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-27, an act to control and regulate the sale of feeds.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to control and regulate the sale of feeds for livestock. It is to be known as the feeds act and, when proclaimed, will replace the present Feeding Stuffs Act.

The first legislation dealing with livestock feeds was enacted in 1909. It was then known as the commercial feeding stuffs act. That act was administered by the department of inland revenue and later by the department of health. In 1920 that act was replaced by the present Feeding Stuffs Act and administration was placed in the Department of Agriculture. The basic provisions of the legislation are to require livestock feeds to be registered, to be labelled to show their ingredients and to meet certain standards of quality and safety.
The last major revision of the Feeding Stuffs Act was in 1937. Since then there have been numerous advances in animal nutrition, in feed manufacturing and distribution and in methods of feed testing which necessitate amending the legislation to keep it in conformity with present practices.
Many of the detailed provisions which now require changing are contained in the act itself. It was felt desirable, in order to permit more ready adjustment of the legislation to changing technical conditions, to revise the act so as to permit many of the detailed requirements with respect to registration, standards, packaging, labelling and analysis to be established by regulation.
The bill now before parliament in no way changes the basic provisions of the present act. It does, however, delete from the act proper many of the detailed technical requirements and provides for them to be established by regulations of the governor in council. In this respect, as hon. members will recall, it follows the pattern used in revising, in recent years, several other statutes administered by the Department of Agriculture.
The house may be interested in a few of the technical changes which have taken place over recent years in the preparation of livestock feeds which necessitate the revision of this statute.
One of the most important has been the introduction into feeds of therapeutic agents for the treatment of sick animals. The authority of the present act is inadequate to insure that in all instances the use of such therapeutic agents is permitted only when there is adequate evidence that they are efficacious, that they leave no harmful residues and that suitable directions for use, and cautions, are carried on the label. Under the bill revising the act there is provision for regulations which will make it possible to keep the requirements with respect to such matters adjusted to changing conditions and practices.
There have been important developments in the use of minerals in animal nutrition

which have led to the incorporation of additional minerals in livestock feeds. The Feeding Stuffs Act contains requirements for standards and guarantees for some mineral feeds but several revisions are now necessary. Under the provisions of the bill there is authority to prescribe these requirements by regulation.
The act now requires all livestock feeds to be registered annually by the department. Twenty years ago there were only about 3,000 livestock feeds registered. As an illustration of the growth and increasing complexity of livestock feeds, the number this year will be over 10,000. This necessitates the streamlining and simplification of registration procedures. The bill will permit these to be established by regulation.
These remarks are probably adequate to explain to the house the purpose of the bill and I will, of course, be pleased to elaborate on the detailed provisions when we get into committee.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF SALE OF FEEDS

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF SALE OF FEEDS
speechtext: No. I think that under this act, because of the necessity for the protection of the general public, particularly in view of the addition to foods at the present time of agents of different sorts, the federal government has sufficient authority to put into effect and to carry out provisions such as these. Also, as the hon. member is aware, the federal government is responsible for standards and under that general provision has been responsible for standards. Subparagraph (b) refers to prescribed standards. The federal government lays down the standards, such as No. 1 wheat, No. 2 wheat, No. 3 C.W. oats, and so on.
